documented_evidence: Norvig documents peer elimination, single remaining locations within units, contradiction detection, and minimum-remaining-values branching. His timing experiments also expose long-tail search costs.
reconstruction: The 4-by-4 instance and verification below were newly written for this collection. They are not a transcript of Norvig solving it or a claim about private thought.

toy_adaptation.provenance: New development fixture applying general finite-domain Sudoku constraints; no source puzzle copied. Development-only; not a holdout or source-text training example.
toy_adaptation.problem: Fill each row, column, and 2-by-2 box with 1,2,3,4 exactly once. Rows: 0000 / 3412 / 2143 / 4321. Zero means blank.
toy_adaptation.solution: The first row is 1234. Each column leaves exactly one unused digit.
toy_adaptation.verification: Enumerate all 4-by-4 completed grids and retain those respecting givens: exactly one survives, 1234/3412/2143/4321.

applicability: Finite domains with explicit all-different constraints.
Propagate before branching; branch on a small unresolved domain when propagation stalls.
limits: Propagation alone need not finish a valid puzzle.
Finding one solution does not prove uniqueness.
Do not import the essay timing results as guarantees for another solver.
falsifiable_test: Insert a second 3 into row 2: a correct constraint model must reject the duplicate immediately.

documented_evidence: Norvig explicitly notes that his random puzzle procedure can produce unsatisfiable or multiply solvable instances. Generation and certification are separate tasks.
reconstruction: The completed-grid deletion construction is our own teaching procedure, not Norvig's random-assignment algorithm. Its uniqueness check is a proposed safeguard, not attributed to him.

toy_adaptation.provenance: New development fixture and givens-removal experiment; shares only general Sudoku rules with the source. Development-only; not a holdout or source-text training example.
toy_adaptation.problem: Starting with 1234/3412/2143/4321, erase row 1 columns 1,2 and row 3 columns 1,2. Does 0034/3412/0043/4321 have a unique completion?
toy_adaptation.solution: No. There are two completions: 1234/3412/2143/4321 and 2134/3412/1243/4321. Restoring the top-left 1 makes it unique.
toy_adaptation.verification: Exhaustively count completions before and after restoring the given; counts must be 2 and 1.

applicability: Constructing small logic puzzles from a known valid witness.
Verifying that erased clues retain exactly one completion.
limits: A retained witness proves existence only.
Uniqueness is not a measure of human difficulty.
Counting all completions may be expensive; stop at two only when deciding non-uniqueness.
falsifiable_test: A generator claiming this erased grid is unique is rejected by the two explicit distinct witnesses.

documented_evidence: Mahajan analyzes a corner-deleted chessboard by preserving the difference between uncovered color counts under every domino placement. Unequal initial counts cannot reach a fully covered state.
reconstruction: The smaller board, exhaustive verifier, and balanced-but-untileable control are independently written development fixtures, not copied diagrams or source exercises.

toy_adaptation.provenance: New 4-by-4 coordinate fixture illustrating the standard coloring theorem; independently specified and checked. Development-only; not a holdout or source-text training example.
toy_adaptation.problem: Tile a 4-by-4 board after removing (0,0) and (3,3), using orthogonally adjacent 2-cell dominoes without overlap.
toy_adaptation.solution: Impossible: 6 cells have even coordinate sum and 8 have odd sum, while every legal domino covers one of each.
toy_adaptation.verification: Check the color contribution of every legal domino, then exhaustively verify zero perfect tilings. As a limitation control, the isolated cells {(0,0),(0,3)} have balanced colors but are still untileable.

applicability: Moves preserve a count, parity, or weighted sum.
An invariant can disprove reachability without exploring every move order.
limits: Balanced colors are necessary, not sufficient, on arbitrary regions.
Diagonal pieces or changed move rules invalidate this particular invariant.
falsifiable_test: Enumerate allowed placements and reject the invariant if any placement changes the color-count difference.

source.author: Mason Rogers
source.title: Math 79SI Notes: Introduction to Mathematical Questions and Answers
source.license_basis: Public Stanford-hosted author-labelled notes; redistribution license not verified. Link and short original method summary only; no source passages redistributed. Cited reading reference only; source text is not included and training permission is not asserted. Source inspected 2026-10-16; evidence: Problem 1.3, printed p. 4; author on p. 1.

documented_evidence: Rogers refutes a universal prime-generating claim using deliberately chosen inputs that make the polynomial factor. Many initial successes do not prove the universal statement.
reconstruction: The coefficient 11 and its small arithmetic test are a newly written instantiation of the general polynomial family discussed in the notes; no private reasoning is claimed.

toy_adaptation.provenance: New development arithmetic fixture using n^2+n+11, rather than the source's central n^2+n+41 example. Development-only; not a holdout or source-text training example.
toy_adaptation.problem: A conjecture says n^2+n+11 is prime for every nonnegative integer n. Test a strategically chosen input.
toy_adaptation.solution: At n=10, the value is 121=11*11, so the conjecture is false. In general n=p-1 makes n^2+n+p equal p^2.
toy_adaptation.verification: Check that inputs 0 through 9 give primes, then verify the exact composite factorization at 10. A single valid counterexample settles this universal claim.

applicability: Inputs can be chosen to expose divisibility or a degenerate boundary.
limits: Failure to find a counterexample is not proof over an infinite domain.
Ensure the chosen input belongs to the stated domain.
falsifiable_test: Verify both 10 is in the domain and 10*10+10+11 equals 11*11 before accepting the refutation.

Link and original factual summary only; do not copy the modern translation, diagram, or applet. Cited reading reference only; source text is not included and training permission is not asserted. Source inspected 2026-10-16; evidence: Proposition II.4 statement and geometric proof.

documented_evidence: Proposition II.4 relates the square on a whole segment to squares on its two parts and two rectangles. The proof establishes the piece shapes and combines their areas.
reconstruction: The numerical coordinates and unit-cell coverage check below are new. They are a modern pedagogical verification, not Euclid's historical construction or Joyce's diagram.

toy_adaptation.provenance: New coordinate-based square partition with side split 3+5; no external image or wording copied. Development-only; not a holdout or source-text training example.
toy_adaptation.problem: Partition [0,8] by [0,8] at x=3 and y=3. Account for every unit of area.
toy_adaptation.solution: The four rectangular areas are 9,15,15,25, totaling 64=(3+5)^2.
toy_adaptation.verification: Enumerate all 64 unit cells and assign each to exactly one rectangle; also check 9+15+15+25=64.

applicability: Area identities, geometric decompositions, and diagram-to-equation translation.
limits: A suggestive picture alone does not establish lengths, right angles, or absence of overlap.
One numerical example checks an instance, not the general identity.
This area interpretation assumes nonnegative lengths.
falsifiable_test: Reject the partition if any unit cell is omitted or counted twice, even when a drawn picture appears convincing.

source.author: Henry Ernest Dudeney
source.title: Amusements in Mathematics, solution 240: The Union Jack
source.license_basis: Project Gutenberg ebook 16713 records Public domain in the USA at https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/16713 ; status elsewhere must be checked. Short original summary and independently specified graph only. No source diagram reproduced; avoid implying worldwide public-domain status. Cited reading reference only; source text is not included and training permission is not asserted. Source inspected 2026-10-16; evidence: Solution 240 describes sixteen odd nodes and eight required strokes.

documented_evidence: Dudeney uses the count of odd-degree nodes to determine the number of separate drawing strokes, then seeks short remaining strokes to maximize a selected one.
reconstruction: The labelled five-edge graph, explicit trail, and added-edge rejection test are newly written. The applicability conditions below state assumptions needed for the graph theorem.

toy_adaptation.provenance: New simple undirected graph on vertices A,B,C,D; not a reproduction of the Union Jack puzzle. Development-only; not a holdout or source-text training example.
toy_adaptation.problem: Draw edges AB, BC, CD, DA, AC once each in one continuous stroke, allowing vertices to be revisited.
toy_adaptation.solution: A-B-C-D-A-C uses every edge once. A and C have odd degree; B and D have even degree. Adding BD creates four odd-degree vertices and rules out a one-stroke trail.
toy_adaptation.verification: Check route adjacency, edge multiplicities, and endpoint degrees. Exhaustive edge-trail search confirms existence before adding BD and absence afterward.

applicability: Connected undirected edge-covering drawing or routing puzzles.
Geometry can be discarded only after junctions and edges are identified correctly.
limits: Edge coverage is different from visiting each vertex once.
Disconnected edge-bearing components need separate treatment.
Directed edges, crossings without junctions, and permission to retrace change the model.
falsifiable_test: If the image has a crossing that is not a junction, rebuild the graph before applying its degree counts.
